utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Krajisnik, the same as every day, you're reminded that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. And Mr. Stewart will now continue the examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I resume the questions, it just occurs to us that developments on Friday afternoon in relation to scheduling Mr. Krajisnik's evidence because of course, we're not in communication with Mr. Krajisnik. It's all been going on without him, the defendant, actually having any idea that any of these exchanges and these orders have been made --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- unless Your Honour would feel it appropriate to inform Mr. Krajisnik of where we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I have to -- Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Stewart asked for more time. I think we granted him compensation for -- for the time we lost at the first day by giving one additional day, and Mr. Stewart has -- from what I understand, intends to ask us for more time. As matters stand at this moment, the order granting one additional day, which brings us to Wednesday included -- Wednesday included?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would mean three days from now on, today, tomorrow, the day after tomorrow, is the way matters stand now. Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There are two matters, Your Honour, we filed a motion to which Your Honour indicated which Mr. Krajisnik should perhaps know. The other which would supposedly be of interest to Mr. Krajisnik is that the Trial Chamber, as things stand, has rejected the Prosecution's application for the time between the close of Mr. Krajisnik's evidence and the beginning of cross-examination, so as matters follow immediately, the one on the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I should have informed Mr. Krajisnik that where the Prosecution asked for a couple of days to further prepare, the Chamber has denied that request. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I ask something of you? I don't want to interrupt Mr. Stewart later on. I have a request to make. I'd like to intervene with respect of the record. When I gave the statement about Trovrh, I mention Veliki Zep by mistake. I said that my part was, first of all, Veliki Zep, that is indeed a repeater station in the municipality of Han Pijesak, but Trovrh is between Pale and Gorazde, that border. So the part relating to Veliki Zep I made a mistake there. It has nothing to do with the answer related to Trovrh itself. And a second point. I made several slip of the tongues when I said -- when I meant prison cell, I said "office" so could that be corrected, please; that was a mistake on my part. I would also like to ask the Trial Chamber, if possible, to give me permission to make a brief statement as accused, in the capacity of the accused, pursuant to the right you accorded me of being able to ask the witness questions from my position in the accused's seat. So thank you, Your Honours, for giving me the floor, and that's my second request later -- for later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik. First of all, the corrections are on the record, so they are there. Yes, about the statement, we'll consider that. It's foreseen in the Rules and there is a practice in -- developed in other Chambers that at the very end of the case that they allowed an accused to make a short statement. Whether we'll follow that practice, yes or no, is another matter. So timing might be an issue we'll still have to discuss and whether at all, because the -- when an opportunity was given, you didn't use that. This is not to say that not another opportunity will be given to you, but that's for the Chamber to consider. But your request is there and we'll inform you about it. Did you, yourself, have a specific idea on timing. Would at the very end of the case something that was on your mind or would you -- because the Chamber might be reluctant to do it too close to your testimony in order not to have matters confused, that you're now speaking as a witness, whereas an unsworn statement, from what I understand you'd like to make, should be well separated from your testimony as a witness. Did you have anything in mind as far as timing is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, linked to the instructions and guidelines that you gave me or, rather, the Trial Chamber gave me, I just wanted to say something in that connection. I was thinking along procedural lines, that I should sit over there as the accused, ask what I have to ask for five minutes of this witness, the place here, et cetera. Just an explanation that would be useful to me. I'd have to consult my Defence counsel, but I can't do that in this position, so that's it. Your Honours, I'd like this to be before I complete my testimony, so not at the end of my testimony, but before I complete my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you'd like to make it part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not as a witness, no. I would like briefly to remind you of the instructions the Trial Chamber gave me as the accused. Now, the -- there isn't an accused now, he's not over there, he's over here. So what this courtroom needs now is that accused over there, that's all we need in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. I also understand that you, more or less, request to have an opportunity to discuss this with counsel, perhaps because -- counsel will certainly understand that having an unsworn statement somewhere in the middle of a testimony is -- is, perhaps, not the most likely course to take, but you'll have an opportunity to discuss this -- you'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll have an opportunity to discuss this briefly with -- with counsel during one of the next breaks. That's on the record as well. Mr. Stewart, please -- oh, yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In connection with the matters discussed earlier and just so the Court is not caught by surprise, the Prosecution would also ask for an opportunity to re-address the issues raised in Friday and addressed by the Court's response on Friday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's on the record as well. Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have brought the map here with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I learned from the registrar that you have brought the map indicating the road between -- the road the convoy had taken, although I also saw that not the whole of it could be on the map. But at least it's, could I say, a northerly route around the city of Sarajevo, all on Serb territory --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I take a look at that, Your Honour, and when I'm next on my feet perhaps I could then deal with it. Now is not a convenient time as far as the Defence are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I asked because I thought that to be a proper way of doing it. I first asked Mr. Registrar to make copies of it so that we -- but you may have a look at it at this moment, that's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, no doubt Mr. Josse and I can have a while of innocent interest over the last five minutes' transcript of the Rules, Your Honour, and come back to those matters in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I was either coming on to or had just come on to presidential meeting which was held at the beginning of -- or early in June 1992, on the 10th of June. It's the 5th Session of the Presidency, and it's P64A, bundle 25, tab 730. It's also in P65, bundle 12, tab 157, the ERN is 00837972. That's the -- that's the English ERN. I don't think the B/C/S ERN is needed immediately. We have it if it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could Mr. Krajisnik be given that? [Trial Chamber and registrar confer].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. Now, do you see it's five people listed as president, including yourself. And then immediately after that it says: "At the beginning of the session, the Presidency reviewed information received during the night," it must be the night, "at the situation at the front and reports of the international," it reads "public foreign press," in the English, but I think the sense is pretty clear. Mr. Krajisnik, did anybody in particular among the leadership deal at that time with reports coming in from or in the international press?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I can't give you an answer as to who could have provided the information and what the information was about, but I do believe that at that meeting somebody was supposed to be there who wasn't recorded as having been present, somebody who wasn't listed, and perhaps he informed the meeting. As I said, there were always more people attending these meetings than was recorded in the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection of what the reports from the international media were about at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this was - how shall I put this? - very unprofessional in operational terms. It was more on the basis of what could be heard, learnt, that kind of thing. I'm quite certain that it wasn't a piece of information or report that had been compiled. Quite simply, there was a discussion going on, and if anything -- anybody knew anything more about the matter under discussion, then they would say. But as to the information media, I don't know, unless it was the Ministry of Information that knew something more about this. So what I'm saying is this: It might have been individual pieces of information presented at meetings of that kind regarding this topic that we were pre-occupied with, and we, ourselves, couldn't receive enough information. So if anybody had anything to volunteer, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then further down in this minute, it's after the 12 numbered points, and it says: "The Presidency agreed with the draft decree." And I want you to go down to where there's a list of six people. Do you see that, Mr. Djukanovic, Poplasen, and so on, there's a numbered list of six people. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's introduced by: "At the session the list was compiled of commissioners of the SBH Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina leadership. The following persons were appointed commissioners," and then they're listed. And we've heard something about that. Did you have any hand or involvement in the selection of those six people to be commissioners?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this meeting. No, I did not have any hand or involvement in it. Now, this group of people, not everyone, not Mr. Tintor, for example, or Mr. Veselinovic, but the four others before that, Mr. Djokanovic, Poplasen, Mucibabic, and Radovanovic, they were cadres which Mr. Koljevic proposed, that that be some emissaries of the state leadership or commissioners. And at the time Mr. Djukanovic -- I heard this for the first time then, that some sort of decision should be taken with respect to commissioners. He testified here that he had discussed it with Mr. Karadzic and that they were appointed as commissioners at the time, and he talked about that decision. When I said a moment ago Professor Aleksandar Buha, for example, that there were people in addition to these persons and Djukanovic himself said that he attended the meeting when this matter was discussed. So as I said a moment ago, there were more people attending than was recorded in the minutes. I had nothing to do with these appointments at the time, nor did I know that a decision about commissioners would be taken and that the decision on the Presidency would be revoked. I just listened about -- to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there at that time any suggestion that you would have a -- a specific role yourself in relation to those commissioners?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was not. That came under the competency of the president, and Mr. Koljevic was charged by the Presidency at that time, in the name of the Presidency. And up until that contentious meeting that was discussed here a number of times, when they sort of said that I should take over that duty, and I can explain that here if you want to hear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We'll come to that, Mr. Krajisnik, it does come up in a later meeting. In this minute, after those six names, it continues: "At the session the Presidency issued the following assignment." And then Dr. Plavsic is given an assignment. And then Mr. Koljevic, it says: "To report to the War Presidency and influence the creativity of the SBH media." Mr. Krajisnik, what do you understand by the reference there to the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the mention of "War Presidency" is a term which was freely introduced there, without any foundations. There was an armed conflict on, so the person who wrote this -- well, it would have been immaterial to him whether it was a Presidency session or a War Presidency session. That's just a mistake, a mistake that it was normal to make because we were talking about a time of war. There was a war on. So the person writing this didn't take care to write "Presidency," but just sort of thought because there was a war on they wrote "War Presidency." A War Presidency never existed, so this term is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was that term, and you've obviously got it in your own language there as it was in this document, was that term, in fact, ever used in discussion among any of the leadership or those working around them?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. The correct term was always "Presidency," although I don't exclude the possibility that someone might have said "War Presidency" on a municipality level or whatever. And for purposes of illustration, in war there were two words that were most frequently used as adjectives. Serb or Serbian, like Serbian force or Serbian lands and so on, and war, a war situation, a war event. That was the nature of the times. It imposed terminology like that which didn't correspond to the truth, nor the situation as it had been established. I don't think any of us would say "War Presidency," although I don't exclude the possibility that somebody might have made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I've finished with those minutes for the moment, Mr. Krajisnik. Could you be given the minutes of the government meeting, 25th government meeting, that's the 10th of June, 199 --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, might I just be allowed to add something in this context, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sure the Trial Chamber will allow you to do that, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A moment ago you asked me whether I had anything to do with the commissioners. Here we can see that it was Mr. Koljevic's assignment to complete the work started in Vogosca with respect to commissioners and the commission, which means that he was in charge of that prior to that, not anybody else. So I just wanted to draw your attention to that matter, that he was given this assignment on behalf of the Presidency, to deal with commissions and commissioners.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was the commission which is recorded here as having been started in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, two notions or two institutions having mixed up here, Presidency and commission. There was action underway to establish a Presidency, pursuant to the decision taken. This assignment was not completed by Mr. Koljevic. Now, since commissioners were the subject of discussion here, the recording clerk wrote down that the work should be completed. Now, as the Presidency didn't exist after this date, he wrote it down as the nomination appointment of commissioners for the commission in Vogosca. So he had been working on that as an assignment of his beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you know about the commission in Vogosca at the time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know about it. All I'm saying is that I know that Mr. Koljevic was put in charge of that, that matter, so I'm just drawing your attention to the fact that it was his duty and assignment before this date and after this date. But it refers to a municipality commissioner, office, or commission, which replaced the Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Mr. Krajisnik, I've finished with that minute unless --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I have not found any reference to Vogosca in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, it's in -- we -- we looked at those six numbered names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then the next bit, I had asked Mr. Krajisnik about the War Presidency and then it's -- in the English it's the next dashed insert: "To complete work on the commission started in Vogosca." Does Your Honour see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I now see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's immediately following -- that's what Mr. Krajisnik has in mind. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I was going to the minute of the 25th government meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stewart, have you given a list of the -- of the exhibits you're going to use to Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, so far as I'm aware we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can imagine, if I look at the time, that Mr. Registrar has found no time to really work on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, may I say that I believe - I stand to be corrected as always, Your Honours - but I believe that this part of the list we're on was on the list before on the weekend. So it might be we've an overlap, which seems a reasonably sensible course, between the list we submitted last week. We haven't got at the moment, I think, all that near at the end of the list that we submitted last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just for practical purposes, looking at the length of the list that -- for Mr. Registrar to prepare every sitting day and then to put it back again might be rather time-consuming.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, Your Honour. We'll help if -- I have limited detailed familiarity with the precise way in which Mr. Registrar deals with papers, but, Your Honour, we thought that the more advance notice we gave and the longer list of items that we would, for practical purposes, definitely come to, the more helpful that would be. But we're always willing to adapt, Your Honour, but we had thought that would be the most helpful course. [Trial Chamber and registrar confer].

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I was just waiting. Is everybody caught up? Mr. Krajisnik's got the document I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I want to ask you -- well, I didn't in the end. I suppose everybody's got it. I didn't in the end of all that give the references. It's P64A, binder 25, tab 678. It's ERN 01245359. Mr. Krajisnik, under item 6 of the actual minutes after we go past the agenda it says: "The following conclusions have been made, that the Ministry of Justice should make a report about the prisoners." Do you find that -- I'm sorry, it's item 7. I'm sorry, I didn't notice the subheading at the bottom of the page. Item 7: "The Ministry of Justice should make a report about prisoners."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then it continues: "This report should pay special attention on treatment of civilian population, prisoners of war, accommodation, food, et cetera. The report will be considered by the government, after which it would be submitted to the Presidency of the republic." Now, this was a government meeting, Mr. Krajisnik, and you've made it clear in your evidence that you did not attend these meetings. But can you say whether at this time, this was the 10th of June, were you aware of any special concerns in relation to treatment of, first of all, civilian population?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was something that the government decided on its own, independently, because it came under its competence and authority. So there was a constant activity in order to have prisoner exchanges on the principle of all-for-all. And there was an agreement between the Muslim and Serb side which was signed and okayed by UNPROFOR, initialled by UNPROFOR. And as this was not successful, then the government, on its own initiative, organised two or thee commissions which toured the prisons. And later on at some point, I think it was in August, informed the Presidency of its findings, and the Presidency took steps to effect what had been agreed. So this was a government initiative because the other side did not offer appropriate conditions for the exchange of prisoners, and probably they wanted to see what the conditions that these people were living in were like, and also to have a look at the civilian situation. So I didn't deal with this, and as far as I remember this was not something dealt with at consultative meetings but it was something that the government did. So if you don't have a report, you can't have a proper discussion on the subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was -- what was your understanding at the time, Mr. Krajisnik, about in what circumstances civilian population might or could become prisoners in the course of war of this nature?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general opinion that prevailed was this, that the entire population and all the people, all the -- were actually the army, all ethnic groups with the army. It was a civil war. You had the front, but it wasn't a classical form of combat. It didn't -- everybody was in some sort of conflict with everybody else, regardless of age, sex, and so on. That was the general situation. There were very few instances where you could refer to a group as purely civilian, but I never thought that somebody ought to be taken prisoner or put into prison because -- if they weren't guilty of anything. It was only the conflicting parties or the warring parties that could be taken prisoner as members of the opposite side and if they were soldiers or part of the armed forces, although it was difficult to distinguish between civilians and soldiers because even people over the age of 60 or 17 year-olds or however old they were, stood guard in front of their houses or in the trenches. But if you take a group of civilians, women and children, they could not be soldiers, therefore, and by the same token ought not to have been in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At this time were -- leaving aside for the moment, Mr. Krajisnik, the point you dealt with in the previous answer as to it being the government's responsibility, I'm asking you about what you knew. At this time were you aware of any significant concerns that the -- that those taken prisoner by Serb forces included women, children, or anybody else who ought not to have been imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not involved in such matters at all. If you're asking me whether I thought about this as a private individual, as a human being, of course I was concerned. I would have been worried if somebody got into prison or was tortured, especially people who are not guilty. However, the government would have to establish, first and foremost, whether any such thing happened at all. I believe that these categories of people should not have been in prison in the first place, especially because there was this ongoing thesis that people got close to prisons in order to seek security, safety, to get away from conflicts. Mr. Mandic gave an example of this nature. It's not that they wanted to be detained, they wanted to go to the other side. So I was worried as a private individual, not as someone who was supposed to take measures in this respect and who was supposed to be involved in this in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, were you -- prisoners of war are specifically mentioned there. Were you aware at the time that there were laws and restrictions governing the proper treatment of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of any rules. I assumed that there had been rules and that if a person is in prison, then those who keep them in prison should stick to the rules. But I, personally, was never involved in this subject matter. I never read any rules to that effect or any statutes. This was done by those who were in charge of that, but I did assume that there had to be rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you at this time - and we're talking about the 10th of June; the precise day is not so important, Mr. Krajisnik, but that part of June - had you received or heard any concerns that prisoners of war were being maltreated at the hands of Serbs in a -- in an unacceptable or inappropriate way?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is no. No. I am so convinced that I was never informed of any such thing. Had I been informed, I certainly would have intervened in order to have an analysis carried out, if I can put it that way. However, on the basis of this I can infer that a similar type of information reached the government, and then the government sent a commission of its own to investigate these rumours in order to see what the actual situation was and then to inform the Presidency. Perhaps somebody from the Presidency learned something about this and said: Well, investigate the matter and tell us about it, but I did not know about it because this was not my line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- the next government session- and I don't want to ask you anymore about that one, Mr. Krajisnik. The next government session, the 26th Session on the 11th of June is P583. It's ERN 01245362. The first item -- do you have that, Mr. Krajisnik? The --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 11th of June, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The first item which is considered -- it's on the agenda: "Current issue relating to mobilisation," and then after the agenda items are listed it picks up that item 1 again. "The government has thoroughly and critically conducted activities, the measures and problems related to the mobilisation in Serbian republic of BiH. It's been concluded that the successful conduct of the mobilisation we've been undertaking a number of different measures that have been objectively possible in the present circumstances. The government has been suggesting that general mobilisation and it's been trying to satisfactorily conduct it through use of announcements, media, and written forms." Were you involved, in any way, in those steps in relation to mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this was not within my authority. Perhaps I could have attended some meeting, perhaps somebody spoke about this, but this particular meeting, these measures, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then after the next paragraph it says: "It has been concluded first that the law on defence and the law on army should be immediately made accessible to all municipalities." Were you involved, in any way, in making that material accessible to municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this law on the military and on defence was adopted on the 12th of May. Technically, it was the government that was supposed to have this distributed. As far as I can remember, there were some changes made and they adopted a different version of this law. Now, was it this new law that they were supposed to send to the municipalities, I really don't know. But as for the session of the 12th of May, if any of that was adopted, then the relevant services sent this to the municipalities, if possible. However, if impossible, then they could not send it because there were poor communications. At this point in time, it was impossible to send anything to the western part of Republika Srpska, for example, the Official Gazette or something like that. Or unusual ways were sought to send things to these municipalities. So that is probably the reason why the government reached this kind of decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What was the state of telephone communications at that time within -- well, within Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- well, actually, I have an impression, and perhaps that impression is not quite correct. I think that, to put it mildly, it was very, very difficult for us to establish telephone communications outside the Romanija area. But I think that some way was found of sending messages, but these were short messages. As for documents like these, I don't think they were sent. If the Assembly was supposed to deal with something, then the MPs would receive it at the following session of the Assembly. It was very hard to do this, and I think it was very hard to send it to the municipalities because it was so difficult to do. As far as I can remember, telephone lines were down. Sometimes they did operate, though, but it's hard for me to pin-point exactly when this happened. In terms of longer conversations or ongoing communication, no, that was quite impossible. But short messages, well that was possible. How exactly, I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I want to turn then, Mr. Krajisnik, to the 6th Session. You can put that document on one side. The 6th Session of the Presidency, which was the 13th of June, 1992. That's P65, binder 12, tab 161, ERN 00814287.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's quite a short minute or they are short minutes. Five people listed as --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- Present. And two items on the agenda: "Report on the situation in the field. The Presidency read written reports from the crisis areas." So written reports from the crisis areas came from whom?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. As far as I can remember, although it came as a surprise to me, on the 11th of June, the Prime Minister was in the western part of Republika Srpska. And at one session he reported on what the situation was like in that area. So - how should I put this? - perhaps he did present some report or something. It would be good if we could look this up, the 11th of June, the Presidency. As far as I can remember, he did report on being in Bosanska Krajina. So I cannot say who it was that sent that report and what all of this was about, unless I'm right when I say that he had been there and then briefed us about it, if my memory serves me correctly. Now, how he went to the Krajina, I don't know. Probably it was the army that got him there somehow. I don't know. Perhaps I've made a mistake, but as far as I can remember, that's the way it was. If you can find the 11th of June, then you will be able to see the Presidency -- I think it was the 11th of June, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, if it -- Mr. Krajisnik, if you express some doubts, if it helps your recollection in any way, Mr. Djeric was shown as present at the government meeting on the 11th of June, but he's shown as absent on the 13th of June when Mr. Trbojevic chaired the government meeting instead.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that at one point in time until the corridor was -- well, perhaps it was the 11th of June, perhaps it wasn't the 11th of June. If you have a record of the Presidency meeting of the 11th of June, then perhaps you could check whether Mr. Djeric reported on his visit to the Krajina. Perhaps I've made a mistake. I'm trying to be of assistance because I don't have the right answer as to who this could be providing information of this kind, somebody who had been travelling, somebody who was in a position to obtain some information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, you've asked, just so that we can make it clear, you've asked if there's a record of the Presidency meeting of the 11th of June, but we looked a moment ago at what's described as the 5th Session of the Presidency on the 10th of June, and we're now looking at the 6th Session on the 13th of June. So -- I don't want to give evidence, but we can all read, it looks as if --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- Such a meeting on the 11th?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I withdraw that, then. I can check that during the break, I mean what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That would be helpful then, in doubt, Mr. Krajisnik. Is it possible to say -- well, no doubt there was a war on, but is it possible to say that this item: "The Presidency read written reports from the crisis areas," are you able to identify what were regarded at that time as the crisis areas?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not all along the front line, although the entire Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was actually a front line, I mean between the warring parties. There wasn't a conflict going on everywhere at the same time. In some places there were cease-fires -- well, not official cease-fires but, quite simply, there was no shooting. Local people established some kind of tacit cease-fires. So the only thing that was referred to were crisis areas where the Serb side was under threat or, rather, where there were war operations going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it -- it says then that: "Concrete activities of the members of the Presidency regarding the situation in the field were agreed upon." Do you -- first of all, do you have any recollections as to whether any such activities or their, apparently, responsibilities were given to you at that point?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no, absolutely. It was believed that the members of the Presidency should be more active on the ground. Perhaps this particularly pertained to Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic, although in part to Mr. Karadzic, too. But I think it was the two of them for the most part. Quite simply, they should tour the front line and become acquainted with problems and, in a way, boost the morale of the soldiers. But this has nothing to do with the Prime Minister or with me. We had other engagements.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then item 2 the Presidency adopted two decisions, apparently, and I'm looking at the second one. "Decision to ban the establishment and activities of armed groups and individuals in the territory of the republic which are not under the central command of the army and police." Can you say to what extent that was understood by those attending this meeting as a problem?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you have an armed people and when you establish an army, then a problem crops up. It was the municipalities that were financing the army because there were no other resources. Very often many of these groups sort of got out of control from the command, that is. As far as I remember this had to do with something that happened in Herzegovina, I think in Nevesinje or somewhere like that. Later on Mr. Karadzic issued an order stating that an investigation should be carried out and that these people should be disarmed. However, the Main Staff kept insisting that there should be political activity vis-a-vis the municipalities so that they would not -- well, how shall I put this? - they -- that they should not attempt to influence the army, although actually there wasn't this kind of influence coming from the municipalities, but then certain commanders in the field were not very competent. So municipal officials were concerned, and sometimes, due to this concern, they quite simply wanted to give their own views and to raise objections because they feared a tragedy might happen. So this very notion of paramilitary units had a double meaning. If it's somebody from the outside, then they have to be placed under the command of the military; but if it's somebody on local level who wants to behave willfully, that is not possible. Everybody has to be under a single command. That was invariably the view of Mr. Karadzic and of the Presidency as a collective organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you -- you knew of the person who is very commonly known as Arkan at this time, Mr. Krajisnik, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know him. I said that yesterday, here, too. Now, from this distance everybody thinks that Arkan was well-known. I would also like the Trial Chamber to admit this correction. It wasn't that I met him in Bijeljina but in Banja Luka, for five minutes, and this importance that is being attached to Arkan and the way he's being qualified now, that's not the kind of importance he had then as far as I'm concerned. As a matter of fact, I can say that he was on anonymous person. The fact that he kissed Mrs. Plavsic and everybody knew about that, that was politically exploited later, as far as I could see. For me, Arkan was a person like any other person, if I can put it that way. Now, in 1992 when MPs came, then I found out that he participated somewhat in what happened in Bijeljina, even in a positive fashion. But when Mrs. Plavsic came back, I do not remember that at the press conference she spoke about Arkan. I don't know. Perhaps she said some volunteer, I don't know what word she used, made it impossible for members of other ethnic groups to get through and that the door was open and that the visit to Bijeljina was made possible. But anyway, in 1992 I never saw Arkan and I didn't really know him, except on the basis of such examples, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So where in the minute of the Presidency meeting there's a reference to "armed groups and individuals," can you say whether Arkan's name came up in the course of discussion among this group?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall. I am convinced that this did not refer to Arkan and to those individuals of his. As far as I can remember, it had to do with some kind of unit in Nevesinje in Herzegovina that was acting willfully. I think that Arkan was only in Bijeljina and in this eastern area. I think he was in Serbia or in Krajina, but he was not in Republika Srpska, at least as far as I could establish by way of some kind of analysis later. At first he was, and later he wasn't. In 1992, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, when you say that you're convinced that this did not refer to Arkan and to those individuals in answer to my specific question, do you -- did this decision, as recorded here, apply to Arkan and whatever group he had with him?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All people, including Arkan and whoever else. If they were in the territory of Republika Srpska, they could not act on their own. They had to be under the single command of the Army of Republika Srpska and the Main Staff, headed by Mr. Mladic. And that went for all. I mean, that was -- that had to -- that had to apply to all; now, whether it actually did is another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any opposition expressed to this decision within the group that met on the occasion of this Presidency meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Every person, every member of the government, every member of the Presidency, and Mr. Djeric in particular, and I, and representatives of the Main Staff, we all stood united throughout the war, that there can be no special units or paramilitary units outside the single command. If somebody was a volunteer, he still had to be under the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm moving on now then, please, to the government meeting which was held on the same day, that's the 27th meeting of the government, 13th of June, 1992. That's P64A, binder 25, tab 671, and the ERN is 0124 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, having got the document already, I'm looking at the clock, I don't know if -- before we go into the meeting, is that a good point for Your Honours? I'm a bit early, aren't I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're a bit earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, I've miscalculated. I've slipped by 15 minutes. My apologies. I'm going by half-hours. No problem, then. We'll crack on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the -- you had this meeting of the government. I don't want to trouble you on several items on this agenda, but then go to item 7, which go headed "current issues," not in the agenda list but in the actual body of the minute. Do you find item 7, "Current issues"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It says: "It has been concluded that the minister of foreign affairs should send a letter of protest to the permanent members of the Security Council KEBS" -- wasn't that the Serbian acronym for the OSCE, if I remembered that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Boutros-Ghali, Mr. Boutros-Ghali and James Baker, which would emphasise that there are no members of BiH anymore, "that only the citizens of our republic are in the Serbian army, that there are regular units from Croatia on our territory, that a number of persons from Sandjak," meaning from foreign state, that's in Serbia, isn't it, Sandjak? --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... "from a foreign state are on our territory. That the commander of TO of ex-Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is a person from Sandzak, that some of the Presidency members are not its citizens," et cetera. At this point, Mr. Krajisnik, was the -- how was the responsibility for dealing with the -- well, it's particularly the United Nations and the United States here worked out or divided up as between the government and the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this has been properly translated. Whose responsibility? Who was in charge of contacts with foreign countries, with other countries? Is that what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, particularly the United Nations and the United States, that there is -- KEBS included here but I was asking you specifically about United Nations and United States.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two or three, rather, points, places, three individuals who were in charge of liaising with international representatives, Presidency representatives. Mostly this was Mrs. Plavsic for humanitarian issues and Mr. Koljevic and Mr. Karadzic, and in the government it was supposed to be the foreign minister, Mr. Aleksa Buha. And the third place person or place was the minister of information as being the technical facilitator for decisions, communiques, et cetera. Now, you asked about the United States and KEBS. Here the government had its own foreign minister, and he was given that assignment. Whether he did his job or not, I can't, but probably he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you personally still involved with your colleagues Dr. Karadzic and Professor Koljevic in attempts to continue the Cutileiro talks?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. If an international representative would come by, and many of them did come by, then we would sit down with them, have a meeting, and discuss possibilities for continuing the conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you have any other responsibilities in the international sphere at that time, apart from your responsibilities in relation to the European Community Cutileiro talks?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have any other responsibilities, except if an international representative would come to Pale and there was nobody else to receive him, then it might have been me who would sit down and meet with the representatives, see what he wanted, comment, give my opinion, things like that. I never took any decision, but I could provide the individual with information so that the representative would be able to go home, do the job he had come to do, and very often they would turn up unannounced, although that was rare.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then on this same minute, the next paragraph, it says: "The need to quickly determine strategic plans of the republic with regard to territory, borders, relations, and other issues which would be the basis for determining balance of goods and other needs has been pointed out." Mr. Krajisnik, so far as strategic plans with regard to territory and borders are concerned, what were the options or possibilities that were under consideration at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The topical question was always this - asked by the government, the army, deputies, here we're talking about the government - to establish and ascertain why we're fighting, because there were two parallel activities. One was to negotiate, the second was to deal with the armed conflict that was going on. And most frequently I think it was Mr. Trbojevic who said it, we didn't always know what we wanted and that's what he's explaining here in his own way. And here the government thinks it's necessary to have a strategy of some kind, how to continue the fighting which was imposed and how to conduct the negotiations. Because, quite obviously, what we discussed on the 12th of May was - how shall I put this? - our position as to what we should strive for in the negotiations. But this seems to have been unclear in the minds of those who concluded this. So they were lacking in that respect. They had to know why we were fighting politically and militarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then it said that: "The question of having a joint meeting of the government and the republic Presidency has been brought up once more. Reason for this has been the conclusion that the government is not sufficiently informed about the most important issues and that, therefore, it cannot participate in determining the policy and making of the vital decisions which is its legal right and duty. It's been emphasised that having this meeting is urgent and unpostponable." Mr. Krajisnik, that's -- obviously can be labelled a complaint within that meeting, the government wasn't being sufficiently informed about the most important issues. Was that complaint, whoever precisely was raising it, was that complaint within the government meeting justified at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't justified, but it did have a reason. There is great uncertainty in wartime, and the government was not sufficiently informed, just like other organs. I, the Presidency, we didn't have enough information coming in to us. And now it was territorially divided, and it was divided that the Presidency or the president of the Assembly had some information which they weren't imparting, weren't sending on, whereas the process should be the reverse. It should be the government supplying the Assembly and the Presidency with information, but this was sent -- made topsy-turvy. They had no -- turned upside down. They had no information and sought information from others. I claim that the Presidency did not have the right information nor did the president of the Assembly, and that if they did then the government members must have known about it or the deputies, let alone the ministers. So there was a dilemma here, and the dilemma was that information should be disclosed, not that somebody have information and hide it from the others. That was quite wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then there's a -- the next paragraph then in this minute, there's an issue of housing in the government in Bistrica. I'm not wishing to ask you specifically about this, Mr. Krajisnik. It then leads on into the next paragraph which begins: "It has been concluded that this issue should be urgently resolved," so that's the Bistrica issue. "It has also been concluded that a joint meeting of republic leadership representatives and Pale municipality leadership should be held, so as to discuss the aspects of all open issues, disable different objections, rumours, and similar, and to reach an agreement about the current issues of locating republic government in Pale." Apart from, apparently, that issue of the location of the government, what were the issues that needed or justified discussions between the republic leadership and the Pale municipality leadership?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is referred to here is Bistrica, that's where the government had already been for about ten days. But -- or 15 days, a fortnight, I can't really remember. Anyway, it didn't -- the location didn't suit it, wasn't suitable, and it said that the location ought to be changed and that they should go somewhere else, better suited. Now, as far as the Pale municipality is concerned, the leadership of the Serb republic came to Pale. Many people came to a relatively poor municipality, people from outside, and your -- you come there and you're a great consumer and you upset the balance and the way in which people work there. So competencies were intermingled. For purposes of illustration there was general dissatisfaction, local dissatisfaction, or the dissatisfaction of the local leadership with the republic leadership and their attitude towards them and there were protests, they protested very often, and the government said: We have to clear up these misunderstandings, and the misunderstandings had to do with life and work on a daily basis. And I think that we already had the problem of Zepa, although I'm not quite sure. Let me look at the date. Well, I'll refrain from going into that. I know that there were some problems between the government and the municipalities, but the most important problem was that a large number of refugees had come to Pale. I know that there were 14 or 15.000 refugees which was too difficulty for the municipality to assimilate and that's asked for assistance. I remember that. Perhaps there was something else that I can't recall just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At this time, Mr. Krajisnik, which is the middle of June, for practical purposes, 1992, if it's possible to say that one person was the leadership of the Pale municipality, who was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the presidents of the municipalities changed. I can't remember who it was at the time. I know that there were three municipality presidents during the war in Pale. One of them was Starcevic, but before him there was someone else and there was a third person after him so that the leadership was changed because it was a lot of work and people asked to be replaced because they had so many problems to deal with. It wasn't that they were replaced, it was that these people asked to be allowed to step down because they had too much work. There was an Executive Board, of course, and they had an Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, it appears to be on record that Mr. Starcevic was at this time still the municipality president. Did you have any direct dealings yourself with him?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did. I think I had some dealings with him, contacts, not much but I think I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, in this minute about three or four paragraphs further on there's a -- there's a reference to chemical weapons. "The government has been acquainted with the use of chemical weapons on the front in the area of Derventa. It has been agreed that the public should be informed about it and that it should be used for propaganda. Regardless of that, a letter of protest should be sent." Did you ever come across any hard information showing there had been use of chemical weapons?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me where to find that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, it's about four paragraphs on --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the government -- yes, yes, I've found it. No, no, I didn't know about this, no New York City.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. I won't ask you about it then, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- I'm looking at the clock again now, also 15 minutes also later. Sorry, Your Honour, it seems I might have cut off an answer. I didn't intend to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, please complete your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Krajisnik, I might have cut you off?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to indicate something which I consider to be important in respect of these minutes which could be of assistance and it has to do with the establishment of this government commission. That is to be found at --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A little slower for the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A government commission was set up, Trbojevic, Subotic, and Dandic [phoen] were the members. May I be allowed to give a short comment? I think it would be of importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm entirely in Your Honour's hands as to whether it's now or after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it doesn't take too much time, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, the paragraph you are referring to is the two paragraphs we were looking at. It's between the reference to Pale and chemical weapons. Mr. Krajisnik, you were going to say?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It will take just a minute I think. A commission was set up for the depots or warehouses which were allegedly under MUP control, and the goods were stolen. And this was directed against Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Mandic. From this time on -- the commission didn't do anything, but from this time on the conflict began between Stanisic and Mandic, Djeric and Trbojevic. And if you will recall, Mr. Trbojevic spoke about that during his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps, Mr. Tieger, you said you would need five minutes to address the matter about last Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Actually, I didn't specify, but I won't require any more time than that, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it as a custom that you never take more than five minutes. Could you then -- five minutes, then we could do it now and we could even think about it during the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would be happy to do so. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I appreciate the Court's prompt response on Friday and the opportunity to address the issue again today. I hope I have -- I hope I have what will be understood as a balanced and modest request, but I'd like to make a couple of points before that. First of all, I'd like to emphasise again the number of occasions on which the Prosecution brought to the Chamber's attention the -- its concern about the deficiencies in 65 ter summary. At that time, we recognised at some point that the 65 ter summary would not be remedied, but we understood that we were to bring to the Court's attention any resulting problems, which we've done and I'd like to do with a little more emphasis. But mentioning first that there were quite a number of earlier occasions on which we brought to the Court's attention a problem with the 65 ter summary; the Court indicated to us at that time, as I understood it its willingness to allot additional time if we were not prepared to proceed in light of the problems caused. To the best of my recollection, there were virtually no, if -- for the most part, we did not seek to take advantage of any of those opportunities, but we pressed forward on virtually all, if not all, occasions. Now, the problem with the -- and I think that this is a reflection of the fact that the Court understood the problems with not getting a 65 ter summary. So if we had a witness who spoke for two days and no effective or appropriate 65 ter summary had been provided, the Court did not expect us to proceed, but understood that it would be necessary to take some time for preparation. In this instance, that problem has been compounded over and over again. The 65 ter summary we did receive might as well have said, "Mr. Krajisnik will be testifying about virtually every issue related to the case." There was no meaningful way to identify the materials necessary, as would be the case with an adequate 65 ter summary. And the situation is effectively what we would have -- what we faced in those instances with smaller or shorter witnesses but compounded dramatically. Now, we've tried to do everything we could, of course, prior to and during the course of Mr. Krajisnik's examination-in-chief to ameliorate the problem, and we've been far from idle; quite the contrary. And indeed if not for an extreme and significant effort, we would not be prepared to proceed in -- at all within any reasonable period of time and discharge our responsibilities as Presidents and assist the Court in any meaningful way. Now, Your Honour, we of course understand that the Court has responsibilities to fix and maintain the schedule, and we also understand that there are issues that are apparent to the Court that may not be so obvious to the parties in trying to make such a decision. And in that light, we've tried to find an appropriate compromise approach that reflected both the problem that we faced that was caused by the deficiencies in the 65 ter summary and that recognises at the same time the Court's attempt to fix an appropriate schedule. So in that light, we would respectfully request the following that at the conclusion of Mr. Krajisnik's testimony on Wednesday, that the Prosecution would be prepared to give up one of its days and would ask the Court to allot one day so that in that instance the Prosecution could begin on Monday. As I said before -- indicated before, that is a reflection both of our attempt to strike an appropriate balance and a reflection of the considerable efforts we've put in to overcompensate in this instance for the problems caused by the deficient 65 ter. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, our submission is very brief. We submit that the appeal to the deficiencies of the 65 ter is entirely unrealistic. Your Honour, there is a certain unreality about viewing the 65 ter summary in that light in relation to a defendant anyway. When Mr. Tieger says: It might as well have said Mr. Krajisnik was going to testify about every issue in the case, that's effectively what it did say because it's pretty obvious that that is, in effect, that's what's going to happen with a defendant so far as there are matters within his conceivable, personal knowledge. So we don't shrink from saying, yes, that's pretty much what they did said. And we submit that it's almost impossible -- I'm sorry, I don't know what Mr. Tieger could want to say now, but he -- of course he's free to say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The point, Your Honour, is that the opportunity to identify an appropriate range of materials from the vast volumes that might be available is dependent upon the substance and nature of what the witness actually does say, not the topic about which he'll testify, and that problem is the one that compounded the deficiencies in a topical 65 ter, as contrasted with a factual summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That doesn't change our understanding one bit. That's exactly how we understood Mr. Tieger's submission. But the point remains the same. We're talking about whether any Prosecution, with the resources they got, could reasonably have been supposed to be taken by surprise in any way in relations to the preparation. But, Your Honour, that's our submission. That's it in a nutshell, and the Trial Chamber can form it's assessment. So far as the actual time is concerned, Mr. Tieger's submissions and suggestions on timing do pre-empt the decision in relation to our application, which we took the trouble to formulate in some detail in writing this morning and to deal with Mr. Tieger's application without dealing with our application is an appropriate way of dealing with it, Your Honour. They -- as we indicated before the weekend, these two matters are now tied together, so now the whole question of scheduling our application, then Mr. Tieger's application, because logically, in effect, it comes that way, need to be dealt with together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd like to say anything about your own application, then please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, our own application is really relatively full. We would seek the specific information. It has a number of elements to it, Your Honour, and I'm not sure that having a draft --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We received a courtesy copy before your request was filed, the filing of today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we -- if we have not read it yet, then we'll do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I didn't want to take Your Honour's simply repeating an issue which you will have an opportunity of reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore, If you would like to add anything to that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, at the moment, no, Your Honour. But that doesn't mean that I would never want to add anything Your Honour, but that's step number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would never expect you wishing not to add anything at any moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I take that as an entirely positive and complimentary remark, Your Honour. But the appropriate course is for Your Honours to read our written application before we are then are invited to make any supplementary observations. Otherwise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Make any supplementary observations because the Judges have read your --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I was unclear as to whether Your Honours had indeed read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't have any supplementary observations, except for the first step. We would like to have the computer information, the detailed information, which we refer to in that application which we did ask for several days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Then before we adjourn, Mr. Stewart, when I asked whether a list was provided when you introduced the 25th Session, government session, of the 10th of June, you quickly responded that it was on the list. I observed the following, that today half an hour before the session started there was a list listing all of the government sessions on from the first up to the last, which would not guide Mr. Registrar very much in which ones to select for this day. I further observed that on the 19th, that is last Friday, you listed exhibits you would -- in the -- as you said, in the near future would refer to on which the 25th government session, at least no government session of the 10th of June wasn't mentioned. And I did not find that same session on any earlier lists sent to the registrar. So if it appears somewhere, I may have had a wrong impression and I would -- and the Chamber would be happy to be informed about not carefully looking at those lists, apart from whether these lists were sent to the Chamber as well so that they could prepare as well. And if it does not appear on any list before the list that was sent at a quarter to 2.00 today, I take it that we don't -- well, as a matter of fact, the Chamber then doesn't need to be informed about it. And I take it that you'll find your way to deal with the matter together with the registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do I get no response on something like that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I made a few observations --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour it contains an implicit criticism which Your Honour does not allow me to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I allowed you to respond after you have checked if my observations are right. I invited you, if they're not right, to inform us so that no misunderstanding would continue. If the observations are right, that is that the registrar was informed for the first time on the basis of a very, very long list certainly not applicable for exhibits to be used today, that if he was for the first time informed about it at a quarter to 2.00 today, then I left it to you how to deal with it with the registrar. We'll adjourn until 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Stewart, most likely, either late today or tomorrow morning, you'll be provided with the statistic information, if I may call it that way. At the same time, you should not -- you should prepare for all situations, that is, that the motion would be granted, that the motion would not be granted. Everything is entirely open. Since we've got only two and a half days left, you should prepare for -- to prioritise -- to find your priorities in the further examination of Mr. Krajisnik because if you would not do so and if the motion could be denied, then you might consider yourself to unpleasantly be put before a fait accompli.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, thank you for that warning. If I -- I don't mean this in the least bit discourteously, if I say that a positive reason, it wasn't necessary, Your Honour, because we do plan for all such contingencies without, of course, any acknowledgement that our motion is not 100 per cent justified. Of course we've planned rules of contingency and we have -- we've dealt with many unpleasant and unexpected surprises, Your Honour, and will continue to do so as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and we -- perhaps our concern was not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's always appreciated, Your Honour. Thank you. Thank you so much for that. It never does any harm to reinforce and make such a potential fait accompli.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we were looking at the minutes of the government session, the 27th Session, it was the same one we were looking at immediately before the break. And in the penultimate paragraph of those minutes, "the government indicated the need for establishing the bodies and taking over of the authority in newly captured areas, which is one of the predispositions for keeping those areas within the republic." Were -- the government, it seems clear, was receiving information in relation to that. Were you, Mr. Krajisnik, being kept regularly informed about what areas were being captured during the course of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what is meant by this. If I knew, I could give an answer, but I did not receive this kind of information, as mentioned here, that some municipality should have its own government introduced now, but I knew something in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, then that -- that was the 13th of June. Could you be given, please, the minutes for the 15th of June, of the government I'm talking about now, still. That's the 28th Session, and that's P64A, binder 25, tab 672. The ERN is 01245371. Item 10 on the agenda -- and I go to the substance of the meeting where this was discussed was -- if you go on to where the particular items are discussed and find item 10, it's a two-paragraph minute. It's in relation to exchange of prisoners of war. "The government has considered the proposed report. It's been concluded that the issue of prisoners exchange is extremely important, complex, and delicate, and that if sufficient attention is not paid to it, it can cause a number of negative consequences for the whole republic. It has been agreed that a working group consisting of," and it's Mr. Djeric, Trbojevic, Kalinic, Stanisic, Subotic, and Mandic, "should consider all aspects of the prisoner exchange problem." I'll stop there, Mr. Krajisnik. The -- at this point, in the middle of June, 1992, apart from any individual cases that might have been brought to your attention by people you knew, I'm not talking about those, but apart from any such cases were you personally involved in the prisoner exchange problem, as it's referred to here?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then item 11, the second paragraph, second sentence, we can go -- jump straight to that. It says: "On more than one occasion the government has pointed out the," I think the word "need" must be missing from the English, "the need to have a joint meeting of the Presidency of SR BiH, SR BiH National Assembly, and SR BiH government. At such meeting, the position, role, rights, and obligations of all republic-established state bodies established by the constitution and law would be thoroughly and critically considered." So far as you can tell, Mr. Krajisnik, was what was contemplated there a meeting of the Presidency, the whole of the Assembly, and the government?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Djeric is a legalist. He's a university professor, and I remember that both he and I very often asked to have powers strictly set so that the organisation of the Presidency would be right. This is a very good example that shows that there are three organs, the Presidency, the government, and the Assembly, and that there is no expanded Presidency, as was referred to here. Because had there been an expanded Presidency, then Mr. Djeric would say: We concluded at the expanded Presidency such-and-such-and-such a thing. On the other hand, he is not informed about what the Presidency is doing, except that he sometimes attends consultative meetings, just like I do. This shows the necessity of the government to have this kind of joint meeting of the government, the Presidency, and of the president of the Assembly, that we meet up, that we exchange views, and that the ministers themselves receive proper information because he believes that the government is not fully informed about some matters. He wasn't right on that, because as far as I know the Presidency didn't know anything more than that either, and I in particular didn't know more than Mr. Djeric knew or more than the government knew, I mean by way of new information, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, that -- that doesn't quite deal with the point, Mr. Krajisnik, as to whether what had been contemplated here was a meeting which would include all the members of the Assembly. If you don't know, Mr. Krajisnik, that is -- I believe the Trial Chamber would consider an appropriate answer to give, if you simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. What is meant here -- well, the president of the Assembly because it doesn't say: Let's have a meeting of the Assembly. It says here that the Presidency has several members, the Assembly has several members, whereas the president of the Assembly is a single person. And by way of inertia somebody said that this was a joint meeting of all three where there would be a comprehensive view of and so on and so forth. I know that this kind of meeting was held, indeed, that we had discussions. Truth to tell, the representatives of the Main Staff were there, too, and we received information from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Krajisnik, I've finished with that particular meeting or minute. There was a meeting of the Presidency on the 16th of June then, just a note, the 7th Session, but I'm not -- I don't propose to ask you any questions about that particular meeting. And to go then to the 29th meeting of the government, which is -- was held on the 16th of June, and that's P64A, binder 25, tab 675, and the ERN is 01245376. And I want to ask you about item 11 -- not item 11 just as listed in the agenda, but item 11 when we get into the part of the meeting which is a few pages on. Do you see the heading, item 11?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Second paragraph -- third paragraph, I beg your pardon. Third paragraph: "It was decided to prepare urgently platforms for meetings with the army, the Presidency, and with the president of the Assembly." Mr. Krajisnik, do-- was such a meeting or were such meetings held, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember one meeting that was held when the government asked for this, to have a meeting between the president of the Assembly, the Presidency, and the full cabinet of the government, that is, in order to get comprehensive information on the basis of the conclusions reached by the previous government session, that is to say the Main Staff was involved, too, because the government thought that the Presidency and the president of the Assembly knew of it more than they did. And they were interested in what the Main Staff had to say as well because, after all, this was a fundamental issue, how the armed conflict was conducted. So from the point of view of logistics, the government was supposed to be there for the army and it was not sufficiently informed. You can see here, as well, that there are three separate organs and that they clearly highlight that they should meet, not with the expanded Presidency, but with the Presidency, government, and president of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then -- that's all I want to ask you about that meeting, Mr. Krajisnik. Then if we go to what was the next Presidency session, that was on the 17th of June and that is the 8th Session of the Presidency. It's P64A, bundle 26, or binder 26, tab 775, alternatively P65, binder 12, tab 165.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.
