utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You've got that, Mr. Krajisnik, the 8th Session. The -- a couple of paragraphs after the names listed: "The Presidency was briefed on the situation on the front, particularly in Ilijas and Hadzici, where enemy forces viciously attacked our army positions the day before and once again, as many times before violated the truce." And then the following decisions were adopted. And then a public announcement number 2 -- I'm sorry, number 1: "The government drafted a decision to proclaim St. Vitus Day the army's saint's patron's day," that's the 28th of June, isn't it, Mr. Krajisnik, St. Vitus Day?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And we come on to it at a later meeting, but do you recall that arrangements were made for various people to attend various places on St. Vitus Day?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that was agreed upon. Now, was it at this meeting or some other meeting, I don't know, but it was agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- and then on this particular session there was to be number 4: "A proposal was made to reconstruct the government. Minister of National Defence President Karadzic shall conduct talks on the assignment of the ministers of defence to other duties." Were you involved in those talks or such talks?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. This was between the Main Staff and Mr. Karadzic and the government. That's where this problem was being resolved. I followed matters, though, and I knew what the reason was why that had been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- and then item 7: "There were two delegations concluded to be formed to visit -- one to Eastern Herzegovina and one to Bijeljina." The one to Eastern Herzegovina comprised six people, including yourself, you're the second one mentioned there, with Dr. Karadzic. Did that happen that there was a delegation and you did go?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the same time, perhaps on the same day, the government established similar delegations. Now, I don't know whether these were the people who actually went out, but this was the initiative of Mr. Djeric at that meeting, where he said that he had set up these commissions, delegations of the government, that would tour the area. We didn't go to Eastern Herzegovina, no. Trbojevic, Djuric, Kalinic, Novakovic, no. This is a reference to an MP. This kind of delegation, no. I did not visit Eastern Herzegovina with this kind of delegation. Perhaps it was a different group of people, and I don't know whether I was in Eastern Herzegovina at the time. I am not precluding the possibility of having been in Eastern Herzegovina, but not with these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And after these two delegations have been listed here, the six names for Bijeljina, it says: "The Presidency decided to visit Krajina the following week and hold there a session of the Assembly of the Serbian People." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, you have been able to see there wasn't a session of the Assembly the following week. Did -- did you visit Krajina -- well, I'm sorry. A different question. Did the Presidency visit Krajina the following week?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether anybody paid any individual visits, but I did not go to Krajina and I doubt that anyone could have gone to Krajina this time because, as I said a while ago, it was on the 11th of July that Mr. Djeric was there, after St. Vitus Day, after the corridor had been established. So I don't know whether anybody could have gone at this period of time. They -- there would have been an Assembly meeting held there had that been possible, but the Assembly meeting was held only towards the end of July and at Jahorina for that matter, the republican Assembly towards the end of July held in Jahorina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I wonder could you be given, please, the minutes for the 30th government meeting, which was on the 17th of June, and that's P65, binder 12, tab 166, it's also found at P583, ERN 01245382. The -- at that meeting, there was an assignment of various people to working groups. It's towards the very end of the minutes. There are two lists, one of six names, one of five names. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I see it. That's what I meant when I was speaking a few moments ago. I just didn't know that this was the date, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that -- the -- they were work visits to be done in regions, that's what it records, and people assigned to work groups were, and then listed and so on. Did -- was there any report back to -- to you, first of all, you individually about the work of those groups?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't even know about this visit. Perhaps it was at this consultative meeting at the Presidency that Mr. Djeric said that he would go, but after that I don't know and no one submitted any reports to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then just slightly earlier on in this meeting the government passed a number of decisions and they're listed, 13 names, on appointing members to judiciary organs. Did you have any involvement at all in the selection and appointment of those 13 people?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not take part in any of these selections or appointments, and I didn't know anything about this. This had to be done by the Ministry of Justice, and this wasn't much choice, was there. So whoever they found they proposed to the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then could we go to the 11th Session on -- there are some intermediate sessions, but I have no questions on those. The 11th Session of the Presidency, and the 11th Session was held on the 25th of June. That's P65, binder 12, tab 169. The ERN is 00814294. You have that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then the -- it's item 3 I'm looking at, and 3(D) towards the very end, that: "Working bodies of the Presidency be set up at the following session and that authority and responsibilities be precisely divided among the members of the Presidency." Did you receive any responsibilities as a result of any such division?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I mentioned. Very often Mr. Djeric and I suggested to members of the Presidency that they have to be constituted properly, that they have to have working bodies the way a collective organ is supposed to operate. I see here that Mr. Karadzic signed this, although he was not present. We probably suggested to him that this be done. Perhaps he did it, too, because he was also a great legalist and I think he was right. I could not have been given this kind of assignment and this did not pertain to the president of the Assembly. It pertained to the three of them so that everyone would know who did what. If you don't have any further questions, I would like to make a few comments with regard to the previous text before this particular point because I have some comments and suggestions that would be very useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I do have further questions, but not on this particular document, Mr. Krajisnik. So which are the specific points to which you wished to draw attention?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, AD2, it was concluded that on the basis of the conclusion of the municipal assembly of Pale in relation to Zepa to raise the question of responsibility and a request was sent to the Main Staff of the army to carry out a thorough investigation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that they do not have this text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to say that on that day, I think it was precisely that day, Mr. Koljevic at the initiative of --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Krajisnik, can I help the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it not in the same document, just further up as item 2?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Unfortunately the interprets do not have that particular date, but that's what was read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's the same document we were looking at, the 11th Session of the Presidency, 25th of June.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We looked at 3 (D) and it's item 2, just further up the page. I'm sorry. I hope Your Honours don't mind me communicating to the interpreters. I'm trying to help them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik I'm sorry, you -- I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no problem whatsoever. As for the case at Zepa when over 60 people got killed and 45, approximately, of these people were from Pale, this caused a major revolt among the citizens. There was a big funeral that was held. At that time all the Muslims were in Pale, and then from that funeral somebody called Sarajevo and said that soldiers came. And then the Muslim armed forces attacked Pale, and then soldiers were running from the funeral by the church to the front line and five or six people got killed there, too. Now, Mrs. Plavsic was the one who was charged with -- who was in charge of talking to the widows of these men who got killed. Then there was this municipal initiative from the SDS board, that Mr. Koljevic should appoint Mrs. Plavsic the president of the commissioner's office for Pale. And on that day he appointed her head of that organ and also the other people that they had suggested. It was her duty to resolve the question of Zepa, and it was precisely at that time that the Muslims moved out. The Main Staff was held responsible here and the minister of defence was also involved. Mr. Karadzic was not there, but we were discussing these complaints that came in from the municipality and we were raising the question of accountability. Mr. Koljevic provided that. You have that in that notebook that I gave you last time in relation to Pale. Mr. Koljevic signed this decision pertaining to Mrs. Plavsic and the members of the commissioner's office in Pale on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, then can we move on to the 12th Session of the Presidency and was held on the 27th of June, P64A, binder 26, tab 774, or P65, binder 12, tab 171, ERN 00814292.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it. I have it before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We see Dr. Karadzic didn't attend on this particular occasion, according to these -- this minute. And then 1 (A) (B) (C) we see an allocation of delegates to represent the state and political leadership at the celebration, and you're listed as -- under (B) for Ilijas, Momcilo Krajisnik. Mr. Krajisnik, I wonder, could you be given the exhibit which is P529, binder 5, tab 195.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do that, Mr. Stewart, may I ask one question, Mr. Krajisnik, one question in relation to your last answer. You were talking about this -- let me just find it -- you talked about 60 people that got killed at Zepa. It's not entirely clear to me, were these Muslims being killed, Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serbs. Serbs, who were killed, and 40 of them or over of them were from Pale. There were some from Sokolac, et cetera. And there was the burial and funeral service in front of the church.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were they killed in combat or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. They set out towards Veliki Zep to take food to the soldiers. There was no fighting, and they had reached an agreement with the Muslim side, but nevertheless they waylaid them in an ambush and killed them all and one of the witnesses who were supposed to come here was a member of the group who was otherwise killed. He, himself, survived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That clarifies the issue for me. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I -- you've just been handed a document which should say at the top "29/06/92" and have a reference to Ilijas Radio or Radio Ilijas. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have read this document. I know about it. I have had it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, rather than me read what's 20 or 30 lines, is it -- as far as you're concerned, is it an accurate report of events on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The qualifications given in the information about the Crisis Staffs that here Momcilo Krajisnik contacted the Crisis Staffs is wrong, that is incorrect. You see, I was in charge of attending the ceremony in a municipality which is close to my own municipality, in Ilijas. This is from the Presidency meeting, and I was there. Mr. Koljevic was supposed to be there as well but he wasn't, and I'll tell you why he wasn't. I was in Ilijas, and after that I went to have a cup of coffee in the office with the people who were in the civilian leadership, which was the Crisis Staff. So the only contacts I had was that -- were that. Here it says he visited the Crisis Staff and informed himself -- well, that was the way this person on the radio conveyed this because he wants to make a news item. He can't say when to have a cup of coffee. Now, let me tell you why Mr. Koljevic wasn't there. On the 28th of July, at the airport and in Lukavica, an agreement was signed to hand over the airport. And Mr. Karadzic was there and so was Mr. Koljevic. And on that occasion a day before or that particular day, the president of France, Mr. Mitterand, landed there, that's how I knew they were there, whereas I was in Ilijas. I have the SRNA information bulletin to back up what I'm saying, if you need to have it. Let me just say when I was in Ilijas I sat with them for ten minutes at the most because there was an artillery attack on Visoko from Ilijas and they all had to rush up to the front. I returned to Rajlovac and Pale myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, I'm going to just read you -- it's a sentence or two sentences from the Prosecution pre-trial brief in this case, and it's paragraph 90?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, I hadn't thought it necessary to have everybody dig out this document for the sake of about three lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It says: "As members of the Presidency, both Krajisnik and Plavsic visited Crisis Staffs and received reports from them on the situation in the municipalities." And then in a footnote there is a reference to: "Krajisnik led a delegation of the Republika Srpska Presidency and the VRS to the Ilijas Crisis Staff on the 28th of June, 1992." First of all, Mr. Krajisnik, would -- would you say you were there, that to describe you as having led a delegation of the Presidency and the VRS to the Ilijas Crisis Staff was an apt description of what occurred?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was under misapprehension, the person that wrote this, it's not correct. You see, Nikola Koljevic and I were supposed to go to Ilijas. He wasn't there; I was there. Now, whether I was there to attend the local ceremony of the saint day in the neighbouring municipality to mine. The central ceremony was held at Sokolac, and Mrs. Plavsic was there and Mr. Karadzic was supposed to arrive, but whether he did or not I don't know, probably he did. As I say, I didn't visit the Crisis Staff, nor could I sit together with them because of the bombing. I don't know whether we were there for maybe ten minutes to have a cup of coffee after the saint day ceremonies. I just went by, stopped by, to say, "Hi guys," and that was all. I didn't even stay to lunch, as I say, because of the bombing at Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's -- that was the footnote, Mr. Krajisnik. And then that bit of the text that I was going to ask you about, that: "As members of the Presidency, both Krajisnik and Plavsic visited Crisis Staffs and received reports from them on the situation in the municipalities." If we take it for the purposes of my question that this is applied to the whole of 1992, so my question relates to that, what comment do you have on the assertion that you visited Crisis Staffs and received reports from them on the situation in the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive reports. I might have gone somewhere on some rare occasion, but I didn't go to visit the Crisis Staffs and I did not have any contact with them. They worked independently. If I did happen to be in some municipality, what might have happened was that we had an Assembly there and then met the leadership. I am one of the few people, because of my family problems, who did not visit Republika Srpska. Other people toured Republika Srpska because someone from the leadership had to be seen to visit the area, if that was possible. So my answer was that I was in Pale, and why I was in Pale and why I attended the Assembly meetings was that I linked -- was linked to Pale and the work of the Assembly. So the conclusions on the basis of those observations were wrong, I did not visit them. Mrs. Plavsic did tour and visit the Republika Srpska, but I think she went to tour it. Her aim wasn't to visit the Crisis Staffs; she just went to gain as much information as possible. She would very often go unannounced because, quite simply, she wanted to keep abreast of the situation. But I don't know where she went or what she did there. And she did not inform me once she returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's clear, Mr. Krajisnik, that Mrs. Plavsic was a member of the Presidency, and that's not in issue. But if we take that assertion in relation to Mrs. Plavsic, "as a member of the Presidency, Mrs. Plavsic visited Crisis Staffs and received reports from them on the situation in the municipalities." Overall, is that a fair description of Mrs. Plavsic's activities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not a fair description, but there is a report of the Pale War Presidency, which I attached and handed over to you, where they were informed of certain problems because she was the president of that Presidency or, rather, the commissioner's office of Pale. But I don't know that she received any other separate reports. On the contrary, I don't think she did. That was not her function. Her function was to visit the area and, as a Presidency member, quite simply she liked to pay a visit to the front and the soldiers to see what their situation up there was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then, Mr. Krajisnik, if we can go to the Presidency session that was held on the 3rd of July. That's the 14th Session --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise, Mr. Stewart, but may I just say something? Your predecessor gave the task of interviewing the Crisis Staffs, and you have a great deal of reports showing that the Crisis Staffs worked autonomously and made independent decisions without informing anybody, and that included Mrs. Plavsic, particularly not me. I do apologise for having to add that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, Mr. Krajisnik, as I was saying, the 14th Session which is P64A, binder 28, tab 809, and also to be found at P655, binder 12, tab 172, ERN 00837970. That was recorded as attended by the five, Karadzic, Plavsic -- I beg your pardon, Karadzic, Plavsic, Koljevic, and Krajisnik. Mr. Djeric is not shown present at that meeting. And then: "After discussion the Presidency adopted a stand for talks between the delegation of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Lord Carrington and Mr. Cutileiro regarding the resumption of the conference on Bosnia and Herzegovina." Mr. Krajisnik, was the -- were the Cutileiro talks at all active or were they really completely in the doldrums at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think that the communications did exist and they were very weak and we insisted here on the continuation of the conference, which existed, in the desire to do the work we had agreed upon, to have Bosnia transformed and a proper solution to the crisis found.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then item 2 -- it says, "The Presidency adopted the following decisions and conclusions." Item 2: "The Presidency issued an order to the MUP, Ministry of the Interior, of the Serbian Republic of BH to conduct an investigation into the activities of paramilitary units on the territory of Gacko and Nevesinje municipalities. It was said at the session that the Presidency was receiving reliable reports that groups on that territory which were not under the command of the army or the police were terrorising and taking vengeance on the civilian population. The MUP was, therefore, given the task of investigating and preventing the activities of these independent groups." Do you -- do you recall where these, described as reliable, reports came from?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "Unconfirmed information." All this is lacking here is the "un," unconfirmed. Now I can answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, I see, well that's quite an important correction then, isn't it? Is that -- in that paragraph you're saying it was said -- can you just make absolutely sure we get it right. Can you read the first sentence of the second paragraph under item 2, the one that starts: "It was said at the session ..." Can you just read it out, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It was said at the session that the Presidency, whilst receiving unreliable reports or unconfirmed reports that groups on that territory which were not under the command of the army or the police were terrorising and taking vengeance against the civilian population. The MUP was, therefore, given the task of investigating and preventing the activities of these independent groups."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That seems to be quite important, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have the original on the ELMO so we check with the original. There is of course no doubt, but the Chamber seeks confirmation of the original to reflect this so there are no mistakes, and then, of course, the next question would be how many versions there are of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's always the question, Your Honour. The question I was going to ask, with Your Honour's permission, to the interpreters, was whether they would in fact plump for unreliable or unconfirmed because both possibilities were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was translated. Could I invite the interpreters to look at the text that now appears on the ELMO, to look at the second part of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- whether the original confirms that the translation, as we receive it on ERN number, last four digits, 7970 is not correct where it says "was receiving reliable reports."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The word is "neprovjerene," unconfirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Anyway, that was the --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Have we accepted "unconfirmed"?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, yes, clearly we have and you seem content --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I -- in order to avoid whatever problems at a later stage, could we have a corrected translation here? I'd rather not correct it myself, such a vital issue. I'll do it on my copy, but at least that Mr. Registrar has one --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There seems to be -- I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It seems to be true -- there are I am told from behind from Mr. Josse, there are two translations it seems --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse is nodding no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Highly --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He's nodding no, is he? Ha.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was going to say it's rather unlikely since this is a CLSS translation that, I believe, was provided very early in the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please take care, Mr. Tieger, where there are -- I don't know whether there are different sources for the same document, that -- but wherever it appears that Mr. Registrar is provided with a correct translation. Because if we start -- if we start correcting ourselves in the originals, that on such a vital matter. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, it had been thought that there might be a second version of the minutes that caused the confusion, so that's all sorted as far as the number of translations is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, it's a translation -- it's a mistake. Of course it doesn't say that the unconfirmed reports are, for that reason, correct -- uncorrect. That's a matter still to be considered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, Your Honour. Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Mr. Stewart. I just wanted to know from you whether Mr. Krajisnik remembered where -- what these unconfirmed reports were? Does he remember this being discussed and does he remember who wrote these kind of reports and whether this issue was discussed, the fact that these were unconfirmed reports? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very often I attended meetings of this kind, that is to say consultative Presidency meetings, and it says "Presidency" here, at which unconfirmed information arrived, which was worrying. And then a commission would be sent out and somebody put in charge of checking the information out to establish the truth and then to come back to the Presidency so they could decide what information -- what steps should be taken. Here it says "unconfirmed information" because there was a delegation that had talked to Herzegovina, perhaps, and you can see that on the basis of other items and received information about that. I know what this was about. There was a unit that was called Karadjordje, we learned that later on, and people went around in a rather arbitrary fashion. They wanted to be something apart from the army and apart from the command, and the commander of that unit died soon afterwards and the situation was dealt in that way, unfortunately, through his death. But what we're talking about here is unconfirmed information which, unfortunately, later on were quite close to the truth that something like that was actually going on when the MUP had checked it out, once the MUP had checked it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik, I was asking you who provided this kind of report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's like this, you know. The meeting here with four or five people, there were always other people attending such meetings which were not recorded in the minutes. And I assume that this other person not recorded here said that the situation was such-and-such, and then we would put somebody in charge of checking it out. I know there were never just four people attending meetings of this kind; there would be other people present but their names were not recorded in the minutes of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one additional question to -- since you have a clear recollection of the issue, you told us what it was. Do you remember who then reported this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, very often --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Krajisnik. Do you know who did it? If you don't know, please tell us you don't know. Not what often happened --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can take a guess. The vice-president of the Assembly was Branko Simic. Quite possibly he had received some information from someone from Herzegovina because the whole subject matter was linked to Herzegovina, it had to do with Herzegovina. So I don't know who it was, but possibly that was how it came about. And this man, he was from Herzegovina, Branko Simic. I'm trying to remember as much as possible, but I don't want to engage in guesswork, of course, and say things I don't exactly know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not inviting you to do so. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, may I hand to you, because I've got a copy ready for you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's an exhibit -- it's already in evidence. It's P64A, binder 28, tab 810, and Mr. Sladojevic has handed to me as I speak lots of copies in English of that document, certainly enough that -- that's the B/C/S for Mr. Krajisnik - certainly enough English copies for anybody who could conceivably be interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, do you see this is dated the 3rd of July. "Order to conduct an investigation into paramilitary group activities in the area of the Gacko-Nevesinje municipalities. Ministry of the Interior is hereby ordered to conduct an investigation into paramilitary group activities into specified areas. And after the investigation is complete, the ministry shall submit an exhaustive report to the Presidency on the established state of facts in the area on the two municipalities." Do you remember if such an exhaustive report was actually produced?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember the report, but I probably heard from the vice-president of the Assembly about all of this, what I referred to a few moments ago. I don't remember this order, though, because it was after the meeting that the order was written; Mr. Karadzic wrote it. It wasn't that the order was passed by that session. It was simply concluded that that should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, when -- the description in the minute is of unconfirmed reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we just --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you say -- let me just check. You said: "It wasn't that the order was passed by that session. It was simply concluded that that should be done." Now, if I read the order it says that "the Presidency adopted at its session on the 3rd of July the following." I have -- could you assist me in reconciling your testimony in that decision that such a thing should happen and it was not decided in that session with the text of this order, which, at least in English, says clearly that this -- this order was adopted at its session, which suggests at least, unless I misunderstand the English language in this respect, that it was done during this session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have interpreted this perfectly. You saw that Mr. Karadzic was not present at the session of the 3rd of July, and he was the one who signed the order. And he signed the order relying on some document, and that is to say the session that he did not attend. He signed it and he said in relation to that session. He could have said that the order was passed I don't know how, but at any rate it would not be the same without his signature there. Had he been there, it would have been different, but then he signed it later, however relying on the record of the meeting that referred to what was to be investigated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the minutes of the 3rd of July say that he was present. Now, your answer very much relies on -- that he was not present, but that's not what the minutes say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I should have a look. Perhaps I made a mistake. Perhaps I made a mistake. If I made a mistake, I do apologise, but could I please have a look at the 3rd of July. Please? The record?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I had drawn to Mr. Krajisnik's attention that very obviously Mr. Djeric doesn't appear as present, but the 3rd of July, yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you had it a few minutes ago, Mr. Krajisnik, it was the 14th --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- The 14th Session -- sorry, I thought you still had it in front of you, Mr. Krajisnik. You see, 14th Session of the Presidency you have, attended by Dr. Karadzic, as His Honour correctly points out. Plavsic --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm sorry. This is what I wanted to say and I made a mistake. In the text it says: It was established at the session that unconfirmed reports are being received and so on and so forth in respect to the civilian population, so I got this confused with the order. And then on the basis of this Mr. Karadzic wrote the order, that this should actually be done. Please have a look. So the Presidency is issuing an order to the MUP here because this has been established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The matter --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I created a bit of confusion, didn't I? I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The matter is clear now. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise for creating this confusion, because there were records where he had not been present and then he did things subsequently. Please, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was the -- when there was paperwork to be done by way of formal orders, as we see here, was that paperwork generally done during the meeting? Before or after the meeting? What -- was there a practice?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not during the session, so it could have been only later, and it was done in the office of Mr. Karadzic. There were some orders that were made that never appeared before the Presidency. He had the right to do that. He worked autonomously, and there is nothing wrong with that method of work. There was no typing at the session itself, and he did not sign documents at the sessions either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, in the minute, the item under discussion, those unconfirmed reports, were that groups were "terrorising and taking vengeance on the civilian population." What was the -- what was the nature of the activities that were being reported, albeit unconfirmed, as being done by these groups?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it mostly had to do with wilful behaviour, not recognising the army. They terrorised all equally, Muslims or Serbs. I don't know. Quite simply, they behaved willfully, that was the kind of information that was received, if I can put it that way. And Serbs complained, Serbs who lived there, that, quite simply, they were a foreign body that respected no one. And since people were complaining, they were certainly bothering the Serbs and the Muslims, too, I'm sure. I cannot pin-point this exactly, but I remember that there were these complaints, this Vojvoda Radovic, I remember that person. He was a good soldier, but he tended to behave willfully and he ultimately got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, what I'm inviting you to do is give the Trial Chamber a picture of what was the degree of terrorisation or taking vengeance.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the degree was, but even when there was mention of similar activities, criminal activity, not to say crimes, whenever I was present on such occasions somebody would invariably be given the assignment to investigate this and to have all measures taken by the judiciary and the MUP and to have the perpetrators punished, absolutely. You can find that in each and every record. I never attended a meeting where there were unconfirmed reports of this kind and when a conclusion was not reached to look into the matter and to punish the perpetrators. That's what the government did, too. These people were not friends of the Serbs; they were friends of themselves and of illegal activities. And this was the response even to minor offences, let alone large-scale activities. I do not remember a single meeting where this would be mentioned and where appropriate measures would not be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In this particular instance, did the terrorisation and taking vengeance that was being reported in an unconfirmed way include killings?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In war, vengeance can be suicide. What is vengeance? If somebody gets killed, then one takes revenge. This is my free interpretation. Terror is torture over certain individuals; that was the vocabulary that was used. Possibly it was different, but I am saying how these two words were interpreted most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me a moment, Your Honour. [Defence counsel confer].

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's suggested that the -- that the -- the Serbian word might not have been appropriately interpreted as "suicide." That's the suggestion I get from Mr. Sladojevic. Obviously I don't know, Your Honour; I only see the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's the very beginning of that answer. It's line 22, Your Honour, page 68, line 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Could you please repeat your answer, Mr. Krajisnik. You said: "In war, vengeance can be" what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vengeance can be revenge on account of a killing. Somebody is killed, so by way of retaliation there is revenge that involves killing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, we must have misheard. We apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The matter has been clarified. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, not confining this question to meetings of the Presidency or any other group that you attended, did you at any time turn a blind eye to reports that had any credibility that there was terrorisation or violent vengeance by Serbs against members of any other ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. I can give several individual examples by way of explanation, but I never heard any information of this kind. If I had heard any such thing, I would have asked for an investigation. And I must say that at all meetings people shared my view. I'm not trying to say that it was only my view. There were such cases when we received this kind of information or misinformation, but an investigation would be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In the same minute, Mr. Krajisnik - I hope you still have it in front of you - the 14th Session, 3rd of July, item 7 says that: "It was concluded that responsible organs shall urgently take the harshest measures against the perpetrators of criminal offences and persons spreading disinformation and panic among the population." Mr. Krajisnik, did that reflect some particular incident or outbreak of incidents at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This reflects a phenomenon. Perhaps there was a specific case or particular incident, but information was being received. There are two matters at stake here. Information was coming in to the effect that there was a high degree of probability of a crime having been committed, and it says here that all the perpetrators of such crimes have to be punished. But also there was intentional misinformation that was spread intentionally by some people or, perhaps, without checking this out. And this caused panic among the population. So these are the two things that are referred to here, that misinformation should be prevented and that culprits should be punished. So these are two types of impermissible activity, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then item 12 records that: "It was concluded that Mr. Kecmanovic, Mr. Pejanovic, Mr. Simic, and Mr. Nikolic, and other Serbs should be invited to withdraw from their positions as official bodies in BH or to publicly renounce their role as representatives of the Serbian people in these organs." Was that a decision which you unequivocally supported?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I supported it, although this was not my own initiative, because different information and misinformation was coming in regarding the difficult position of the Serbs in Sarajevo. Formally they were in government in Sarajevo, but they could not do anything for the Serb people. And then a false picture was being created that there was a multi-ethnic government. Some people were there simply to be in high office and others because they couldn't get out. They represented themselves as Serbs, but in actual fact they were Serbs by birth but they only took care of themselves. I have to say the truth, and I, therefore, have to say that they did try to help many people, many Serbs in Sarajevo. I was informed about that. But their possibilities were highly limited, and we wanted this false multi-ethnicity to be unmasked here because it was not essentially there. There was no substance to it. Actually, let me just add one more thing. Mr. Kecmanovic said publicly: "I am a Serb but I do not represent the Serbs." No problem with that because I do not have a mandate to represent the Serbs, whereas they were saying that they represented the Serb people, which was not true because they did not have any rights. They were there only formally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, then, I want to move on to the 15th Session of the Presidency, which was held on the 6th of July. And that's P64A, binder 25, tab 726, alternatively P65, binder 12, tab -- I'm afraid it's either 177 or 174. It's 174. And the ERN is 00837958 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, could I ask one additional question in relation to the previous issue. Mr. Krajisnik, you said -- you were talking about the complaints against, as you said, this Vojvoda Radovic. And you said: "and he ultimately got killed." When was he killed, could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's not that he was assassinated, but he got killed in combat, at the front line. There is a difference. It's not that somebody assassinated him. It's not that a Serb killed him that way, but there were such clashes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was only asking when. Not how, but when.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know it was later, but I don't know. I don't know. I just know that -- well, I don't know when he got killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How -- I'm asking you because it more or less suggested that the issue was resolved by Vojvoda Radovic had died. Therefore, I'm asking when he died. Do you know how much later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this problem was resolved. An investigation was carried out, and the problem was resolved; however, when I was talking about who the commander was, to the best of my recollection, it was this man. And I said that he got killed. Perhaps the problem was resolved. And it wasn't that his death solved the problem, no, the authorities solved the problem. So perhaps it sort of fitted in the wrong way that his death resolved the problem. I don't know when he got killed. He got killed later, but the problem was certainly resolved through an investigation. And there were no paramilitary units. Maybe he got killed soon after that, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the same Vojvoda Radovic as mentioned by Mr. Seselj in this television -- I think it's television speech which is P1090, or don't you remember that? It was a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was during the testimony of Mr. Poplasen that -- because then a Vojvoda Radovic on Podvelezje was mentioned. Is that the same or is that a different person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, since I knew his brother, that's why I remember. I mean, I never met the man, I never saw the man. Is it the same person, is it a different person, I really don't know. My information is very poor, as far as his details are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you said earlier also that one would investigate the matter and people would be prosecuted or punished, something of the kind. Now, was this person who died later, was he -- was he punished, was he arrested, or what happened to him, this Vojvoda Radovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if this was properly interpreted, this is a separate item on the agenda, and I was talking within that item. I was saying that there are two questions here. I have no knowledge as to what happened to this Vojvoda Radovic, whether he was punished, whether he was not punished, whether an investigation was carried out or not. I know nothing. However, I assume on the basis of what I heard, if he was guilty he should have been punished or replaced but I have no knowledge as to what actually happened to him. I don't even know whether he was guilty. What I'm saying now is I know I remember a name; I mentioned him. As for the details, I really know nothing about what happened down there in Nevesinje and Gacko. I'm just saying what the misinformation was I mean -- or rather, this information concerning his wilful behaviour, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed. By the way, we are close to -- we are already very late, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I mention two very quick points before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, I decline to make supplementary submissions earlier, and I'm not going to do that now, Your Honour, in relation to those. But what I ask -- this, Your Honour, that if Your Honours are proposing any answer or ingredient in Your Honour's decision which it would only be fair to allow the Defence to make submissions on, in other words, something that couldn't fairly be anticipated and dealt with our application in advance, then we do specifically request the opportunity to do that rather than find the point for the first time in a Trial Chamber decision. That's point number one. Point number two, Your Honour, is, may we see Mr. Krajisnik in this break to discuss the procedural matter which he raised at the very beginning of today's session? And we would, of course, be careful in the usual way to steer clear of any content which relates to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, I think I already said that the matter raised by Mr. Krajisnik, which we understood to be a request to consult with you was that during one of the next breaks he could see you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We just wanted to be clear that we had that green light on our side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn until quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just before we begin, Your Honour, if I could put on the record that we have provided to the registrar and copies to the Defence of P605, P964, P981, P1021, and P1134. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you for that opportunity. We have clarified, we think, to a considerable extent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, clarified to a considerable extent, we hope, that what Mr. Krajisnik had in mind. It's nothing to do with any unsworn statements or statements separate from his evidence; it's nothing whatever to do with that, as it turns out. It stems from the guidelines and the opportunity that Your Honour has given to Mr. Krajisnik to cross-examine and also in relation to Defence witnesses to ask questions himself, after due consultation with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And he notionally -- as he described this morning, he notionally has in mind being able to ask such questions with himself as the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which comes down more or less to adding anything he think is of importance to add to his testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it does, Your Honour. We had suggested to Mr. Krajisnik, and we steered clear, of course, of specific points, Your Honour, but as a scheme we had suggested to Mr. Krajisnik that it might be helpful if he were to prepare his own note or list of such topics or such matters that he felt at the end of his examination -- conventional examination-in-chief, I hope it's reasonably conventional, by counsel he would still wish to raise. And then we could -- the Trial Chamber is still in control. We can take it from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I hope Your Honour would feel that was at least a useful starting point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, then please make a list of parts that are missing. I hope you will understand that if the Chamber will come with a ruling that time is limited for the Defence, that that is not a way out to answer all the questions Mr. Stewart may have had in mind for six days to come, but if there's any -- any specific matters you think that they should be -- they should be added to your testimony and you would have asked yourself, after consultation with Mr. Stewart, we'll consider you to give you an opportunity to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The only observation, Your Honour, is it would seem to follow what time we did have the shorter Mr. Krajisnik's list would become one supposes, but that's another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I turn then to the 15th Session of the Presidency, that's -- was on the 6th of July. And, Your Honour, that is P64A, binder 25, tab 726, alternatively P65, binder 12, tab 174.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Perhaps I won't -- perhaps I've given that reference. Perhaps we've turned up that document anyway. Not to worry. If we turn to item 4, please, Mr. Krajisnik -- I'm skipping over -- item 3 doesn't mention talks with Professor Kecmanovic, but I'm not going to ask you about that in the circumstances. Item 4: "It was concluded that the president of the Presidency must appoint someone to take his place in case of absence from the seat of the Presidency. The following division of tasks was adopted. Military issues: Dr. Karadzic; international relations and questions relating to information on propaganda: Dr. Koljevic; questions relating to refugees, humanitarian aid, and church contact," I'm not reading verbatim there, just summarising, "Dr. Plavsic." And back to verbatim: "For contacts with UNPROFOR set for military issues, Dr. Biljana Plavsic. Questions related to commissioners and the economy: Momcilo Krajisnik; questions relating to supplies: Dr. Branko Djeric." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, what did you understand to be the task or responsibilities being allocated to you there by saying that you should take on the tasks of questions related to commissions, leave aside economy, questions related to commissions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to ask the Trial Chamber to go into private session for a few moments, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm -- I'm going to repeat my question, but perhaps to make it clear that there are two distinct questions and at the moment I'm asking you the first. The first relates to what tasks you were taking on by this item in the minute relating to commissioners, and the second distinct question is why you were given such tasks. So at the moment I'm sticking with the first question which, as I expressed it before, was: What did you understand to be the task or responsibilities being allocated to you by what is said in this minute that you should take on questions related to commissions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope that I am going to give a satisfactory answer. This fourth item has to do with my assignment, that I should be in charge of commissioners and the economy, that is closely linked to the first item, and that is item 1. And I'm going to quote it now in respect of Mr. Koljevic: "Cannot work for health and psychological reasons. He has family problems, health problems, and this affects his work in the Presidency." This was a quotation. So at first it was for those reasons that he wanted to leave the Presidency, and this entire debate had to do with us trying to persuade him not to do that because that would be detrimental. And then he provided some alternatives, namely that he would stay on the Presidency but that he could be disburdened of those issues that are difficult for him. He did not mention commissioners, though. Have a look and you will see. Later he said that he could not really handle the commissioners. Now, as we were present there, gentlemen, an item on the agenda, that was A4, had to do with the Presidency and the commissioners. And whatever Mr. Koljevic, Karadzic, and Mrs. Plavsic were doing, all of that was what the Presidency is supposed to do. Commissioners and the economy that Krajisnik and Mr. Djeric got with are not really the affair of the Presidency. Mr. Aleksa Buha was in charge of different matters and other people, too. Now, why was it said now that the commissioners should be dealt with is this it seemed that there was no one to deal with that. At that moment, I did not even think about that, that somebody could proclaim me a member of the Presidency, if I took this like: You won't do it, okay, I'll do it to help you out. So I was simply present, and then they said: Can you handle that as an obligation of your own? The situation was stabilised quickly. You will see later through the records Mr. Koljevic continued to work in the Presidency. He did not leave. So this was a family problem that he had as well as these health problems that he had of his own, the tension. I don't know if there was anybody who was working with the commissioners. I did not simply appoint anyone. I did not sign anything to that effect, and I am quite willing to explain why I signed the things that I did sign. If you recall, Miskin Jovanovic and the rest, now, why did I do this? Everyone present here now, if you were to be in that situation, all right, stay here, we'll find someone who will do that. It wasn't the point who's going to work with the commissioners, but just as Mr. Karadzic said it is important for us to exist because that's a symbol of the state. Mrs. Plavsic and all the rest of us were saying that because this was a man who was the legitimate representative in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it would have been a great pity. I assure you that this was not something that had been prepared beforehand, that Mr. Djeric and I would be entrusted with this. What does the Presidency have to do with the economy, and then that's me? If you're receiving someone -- if somebody says: Well, you receive that person. It was no problem for me to help them out. Mr. Koljevic pointed out that he could not handle the commissioners, and I wanted us to overcome the problem at that point so that that would not be a reason for him to leave the Presidency. This is the whole truth. That was the reason. He could not take anymore, so he would not have stayed in this office otherwise. Believe me, he continued doing all this work, but that's the way it was at that moment. And I am saying this before God and before you, that's the way it was. Had I known that somebody would have said that this meant that I was turning into a member of the Presidency, well, no. But I mean, I wasn't asked that way and as if it mattered at that point. And now when I'm supposed to explain it, I see that it's so hard to explain. Especially supplies, the question of supplies, that has nothing to do with the Presidency; that's what the government does. It was just mentioned by accident. So please, you have different records here. Aleksa Buha and others were entrusted with different duties but they were present there. And they were given these assignments, that they were supposed to do something. But it wasn't really a division of duties among the Presidency. And thank you ever so much for having understood the first point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, actually what you've done, Mr. Krajisnik, but it's perfectly helpful, you've answered my second question, but that's helpful because it was going to be the one after my first question. But going back to my first question which is: What then -- what did you understand to be the tasks involved in your taking on responsibility for questions related to commissioners?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding was just that that would be the way for Mr. Koljevic to stay on the Presidency, and then we would overcome that and then we would deal with the situation tomorrow. Tomorrow would be another day. Commissioners, well that would be no problem, but the basic issue for me was -- well, we've eliminated all the reasons you've given to us, so please stay ant Presidency. So that was my reason then. See here, that he would like to withdraw from the Presidency due to health concerns? That is 1(A). Exhaustion -- well, somebody does not have to have a headache or a foot ache in order to feel ill. At that moment Mr. Koljevic was my priority, not the commissioners, and we succeeded, which matters the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was it -- was it intended that -- by what's recorded in the minutes here, saying that you were to take on questions related to the commissioners, was it intended that you actually would, in practice, take on responsibilities in relation to commissioners?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no responsibility there because those commissioners practically did nothing. That was the first thing that should be said. Secondly, if you read the record, before that he had contacts, appointments, whatever, and then he said that that was his reason for leaving. So that was the main point. I will tell you, Mr. Trbojevic said so and all the others. No one informed them. At first Mr. Djokanovic went to a few municipalities, but then he stopped working, too, because people in municipalities were working independently. And Mr. Poplasen also said that he established his own party and that he worked on that more than as a commissioner. Perhaps some logistics was required that people would get a travel order or whatever, but their work was not visible and it didn't really require an effort. I could have done what he did before, but I didn't do it. But even had I done it, it would have been to help out the Presidency, not as a member of the Presidency myself. All of that can be seen from this record, if you analyse it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So when you say there was no responsibility there because those commissioners practically did nothing, was it, at least technically, part of your responsibility to try to see that they did do something?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Karadzic still signed all their appointments. Everything that you saw over there I can explain. I can explain why I signed all of that. As for this, if necessary he signed whatever the commissioners needed on the basis of some proposal coming from the ground or whatever. So what would be the function of that person who would take care of the commissioners? These people should come in, provide information, work, but that's not what they did. Quite simply, they were all freelancing, so to speak, and they were sort of helping out on the ground. They knew what was going on in Pale and then they were sort of helping out elsewhere. So it was not difficult to - how should I put this? - take care of the commissioners. It didn't involve any particular work, and that is obvious. I can also explain what Mr. Djokanovic said about the man from Sarajevo. I can tell you exactly what it was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So in the -- this minute, it's the last item in this minute under item 6, it's the very last paragraph. It says: "The advisor to the Presidency was made responsible for issuing public statements from sessions of the Presidency after first agreeing on the text with a member of the Presidency, Dr. Nikola Koljevic, who was in charge of information and propaganda." Mr. Krajisnik, it may be my failure of memory, but the -- who was the advisor to the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cancar, Petko Cancar --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, it's in number 3. I see that it was me just missing that. He's named in number 3. So that was him. And he was to agree the text with Dr. Koljevic. Was that -- was that then in the nature of a sort of soft job then to keep Professor Koljevic with some task or some function without it being too onerous?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. You can see here, too, that he is being given some importance and some enthusiasm. The advisor is going to write it up and will consult Mr. Koljevic. You put it right. You defined it exactly the way it was, so then this man would write it up and then he would correct whatever's written. So that's it. Once you finish, I would have a few additional comments before we move on to 3, if you're introduced --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, the clock's behind you, Mr. Krajisnik; it's in front of me. So I don't know what His Honour will say about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I take it if you have some comments to make, that it would take at least a couple of minutes. It's 7.00 sharp. If you could do it in one minute, otherwise keep it until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Half a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to draw your attention to the last page, the last point, where it says here under number 5: "The secretary of the Presidency and the Assembly," it was a single person for two institutions, "is urged to draft and deliver decisions to all employees of the Assembly and the Presidency." There were two institutions; that is what I wanted to tell you. In this same record you can see that it was two institutions, it was Milos Savic, but two institutions. That is it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much indeed for your understanding. I would also like to thank the Office of the Prosecution for their understanding, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, my instruction again is that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony but -- already given or still to be given. And we'll adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00, Courtroom II. And, Mr. Krajisnik, most likely, the maps you provided will, by then, be photocopied. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 23rd day of May, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24
